articles.title: Arthur Fery: Lorenzo Musetti awaits in first round of US Open for British No 1
articles.summary: New British No 1 Arthur Fery faces a huge first-round encounter when he goes up against 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti on Tuesday; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Fery returned to British No 1 and set a new career high at No 33 following his run to the Winston-Salem Open final this week. His hopes of landing his maiden ATP Tour title were ended in emphatic fashion by Ignacio Buse on Saturday .

The 24-year-old was aiming to add to his already memorable season having reached the semi-finals at Wimbledon but he was denied by the Peruvian.

Eight weeks ago, Fery was outside the top 100.

Despite missing out on the title, Fery will take plenty of confidence from a week that yielded five consecutive straight-set victories and further underlined his potential on the ATP Tour.

The Brit will now switch his attention to the US Open, where he is set to make his main draw debut in New York.

He faces a tough first-round clash against Musetti, but his recent form suggests he will arrive in Flushing Meadows full of belief and confidence.

Former British No 1 Tim Henman has been impressed by Fery's attributes, telling Sky Sports Tennis : "Arthur has strings to his bow with that speed of movement and recognising when you hit a good shot that you can move forward.

"Given his lack of height and how he struggles a little on serve, he makes sure he uses all of those other attributes - led by his speed and baseline game from the back of the court. Both forehand and backhand are so solid.

"He has got a tennis IQ and his speed of movement, but recognising when you hit a good shot, then maybe the opportunity to step forward and knock that volley off.

"Wimbledon was an incredible achievement but to come to the States and make that final will give him huge confidence, irrespective of what happens here at the US Open. Given his lack of height and perhaps how he struggles a little bit on serve compared to other players, he's got to make sure he's using all those other attributes led by his speed and baseline game from the back of the court."

Laura Robson said it is good to see Fery backing up his Wimbledon run: "It's so good to see Arthur back up his Wimbledon semi-final run so quickly.

"Often, you see players have a shock result in a Grand Slam and it's better than they expected then they adjust to that new ranking for the next few months, so it's great to see him make that ATP 250 final and enjoying it.

"He feels like he belongs at the top of the game."

Why Britain's Arthur Fery could be a threat at US Open

A few months ago, few people had heard of Fery but can he have another big couple of weeks at the US Open?

"His first-round opponent Musetti has a lot of variation and uses the backhand slice and a powerful top spin shot," said Ryan Harrison. "I'm really looking forward to this. It's one of the most electrifying first-round match-ups to see how it plays out."

Tennis legend Martina Navratilova added: "He's quick around the court and really fast moving forward.

"He hits volleys so much closer to the net than other players and that's what makes him such an effective, offensive player."

The US Open is live on Sky Sports from August 30. Stream tennis with no contract on NOW and the Sky Sports App . You can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.

articles.title: Why Naomi Osaka walked onto US Open court in gray hoodie and cornrows
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW DELHI: Naomi Osaka made a bold statement at the 2026 US Open, combining tennis with basketball-inspired fashion as she stepped onto Arthur Ashe St.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Naomi Osaka made a bold statement at the 2026 US Open, combining tennis with basketball-inspired fashion as she stepped onto Arthur Ashe Stadium for her first-round match against Anastasia Zakharova.She arrived wearing a long white skirt and a gray hooded robe covered with newspaper-style clippings. Underneath, she wore a black outfit, while her hair was styled in cornrows beneath a headband, a look strongly associated with NBA legend Allen Iverson during his Philadelphia 76ers days.The four-time Grand Slam champion explained that her outfit was a personal tribute to Iverson, whom she has long admired for influencing sports fashion.“It’s my, I guess, my tribute to Iverson. I really like him a lot,” Osaka said after her 7-6 (6), 7-6 (3) win. “I mean, Nike said basketball, so I said, ‘OK, you want basketball, I’ll give you basketball.’”Osaka had already spoken about Iverson before the tournament, calling him a trailblazer who changed how NBA players approached fashion and self-expression.“I think he’s also someone that I look up to a lot, because he’s kind done a lot in fashion, whether it’s on purpose or not, but he’s shifted the way that NBA players dress,” Osaka said Saturday. “I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports and also just expressing yourself through style, I feel like he’s someone that I look up to in that regard.”Watch:Iverson, who had never communicated with Osaka before, responded to her tribute on Instagram: “Wow, what a honor!! BIG FAN can’t wait to meet you.”Osaka survives tough openerOn court, Osaka had to work hard for her victory. She led 5-2 in the first set and 5-3 in the second, but Zakharova fought back both times to force tiebreaks. Osaka eventually won both and secured her place in the second round.The victory marked her 79th Grand Slam match win and her 29th opening-round victory at a major. She will next face Czech player Katerina Siniakova, against whom she holds a 2-1 career record.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'A big surprise': Carlos Alcaraz makes honest admission on Novak Djokovic’s shock US Open defeat
articles.summary: Tennis News: Carlos Alcaraz began his US Open title defence with a straight-sets win over Roman Safiullin and admitted he was surprised by Novak Djokovic’s shock f.
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz began his US Open title defence with a straight-sets win over Roman Safiullin and admitted he was surprised by Novak Djokovic’s shock first-round defeat.Djokovic lost to Mariano Navone in five sets, ending his tournament much earlier than expected and ruling out a possible semi-final clash with Alcaraz.Alcaraz said he watched the final set of Djokovic’s match and understood how significant the result was.“I saw the fifth set. Obviously it was the first time that Novak lost in the first round here in this tournament, so it's a big surprise. Someone like Novak going out in the first round, it's surprising,” Alcaraz said.However, the defending champion insisted Djokovic’s exit would not change how he approaches the tournament.“But every Grand Slam is really difficult to get through every round, every player. It's really tough. You have to earn the win (from) the first ball until the last one. He was in my part of the draw, but it was in the semis. For me, the semis are too far away, so I just try to go round by round,” he added.Alcaraz makes strong returnThe 23-year-old Spaniard was also dealing with his own uncertainty after missing 139 days because of a right wrist injury. Returning to singles competition for the first time since April, Alcaraz admitted he felt more nervous than usual.“It was a difficult day for me,” Alcaraz said when asked about the feelings ahead of his first singles match in 139 days. “But at the same time, a really beautiful one. Starting the day I was really nervous, thinking ‘I'm going to make it, I'm going to compete again’. I had more nerves than usual, but just happy, because my goal here is to compete, to enjoy, and let's see how my body's going to react after the matches.”Also Read:Alcaraz produced 28 winners against Safiullin and confirmed he felt no pain during the match. The win took his season record to 23-3. He will next meet Portugal’s Jaime Faria as he continues his bid for another US Open title.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Novak Djokovic, un futuro en el aire: "Australia está muy lejos"
articles.standfirst: El campeón de 24 grandes, de 39 años, sólo ha podido jugar siete torneos este curso
articles.summary: El campeón de 24 grandes, de 39 años, sólo ha podido jugar siete torneos este curso
articles.body: Novak Djokovic celebraba en la previa del US Open su presencia por vigésima vez en el último grande del curso. El número 20 persigue al serbio, que se despidió en la primera ronda de un major 20 años después tras caer en cinco sets ante Mariano Navone, por 7-6(5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2 y 6-1. Esa instantánea no se daba desde el Open de Australia de 2006 cuando un joven ‘Nole’ hincó la rodilla frente al estadounidense Paul Goldstein. Con 39 primaveras, el problema ya no es la edad sino que su cuerpo no tolera las condiciones extremas y, en especial, la humedad. Y en el verano de Estados Unidos no se baja del 70 por ciento, ya sea en Cincinnati o en Nueva York. En el Masters 1000 de Ohio se despidió en el debut ante Thiago Tirante, con claros problemas para manejarse con los elementos. En la ciudad de los rascacielos fue otro argentino, Mariano Navone, el que le eliminó cuando nadie lo esperaba. Ya da igual que juegue de día o de noche. Con sol o bajo los focos. Él mismo ya había avisado que no es lo mismo entrenar que jugar. Navone es el 49 del ranking y Tirante era el 50 cuando apeó a Djokovic. Ninguno de sus dos verdugos tiene jerarquía ni tenis para derrotar al mejor tenista de la historia en condiciones normales. Pero Nole está pagando el precio de la alta competición y su carrera está ahora mismo en entredicho. Parece una utopía la opción de volver a ganar un Grand Slam y también el récord de títulos ganados por Jimmy Connors en la Era Open con 109. Él acumula 101. Su motivación más realista es participar en los próximos Juegos de Los Ángeles 2028. “No lo disfruté. Creo que fue obvio que tuve una sensación horrible en la pista para mí. Es algo que he estado cargando en cada partido este año. Todo mi cuerpo empieza a colapsar, básicamente calambres y dolor” explicaba a la conclusión. Vómitos y la presencia del fisioterapeuta, para tratarle la espalda y el hombro fueron la antesala de una derrota entre lágrimas. Su despedida sonó a la última en la Arthur Ashe. Cuatro años después de la retirada de Roger Federer y dos desde que Rafael Nadal dijo basta, ahora sí Djokovic se debate con qué hacer. De momento, no hay fecha de retorno. Y cuando vuelva ya no estará en el top10 mundial por lo que sus cuadros serán cada vez más complicados. Es undécimo y Rafa Jódar puede retrasarle aún más si alcanza los cuartos de final. La diferencia entre ambos es de 321 puntos. Para encontrar la última vez que no estaba entre los diez primeros del ranking hay que remontarse a la semana del 2 de julio de 2018. La pregunta está sobre la mesa y ya se habla en los corrillos del tenis sobre cuándo la leyenda serbia debería dejarlo. “Australia queda muy lejos. No sé qué me pasa ni hasta dónde puedo llegar si sigo de esta manera”, avisa. En la presente temporada apenas ha podido disputar un total de 21 partidos, de los que ha decantado 14 a su favor. Además del Open de Australia, Roland Garros, Wimbledon y US Open, sólo ha estado en Indian Wells, Roma y Cincinnati. El final perfecto hubiese sido con el oro olímpico de París ante un rival de la talla de Carlos Alcaraz. El hambre de seguir ganando le empujó a mantenerse en activo: “Me planteé abandonar el partido con Navone, pero luego gané dos sets”. La magia de la chistera de Nole se agota.

articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz eleva a 15 su racha victoriosa en partidos de Grand Slam, su tope
articles.standfirst: Alcaraz acumula 28 partidos resueltos a su favor en sus últimos 29 que disputó en los major
articles.summary: Alcaraz acumula 28 partidos resueltos a su favor en sus últimos 29 que disputó en los major
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz, con su retorno triunfal a la ATP merced al triple 6-4 que le endosó al ruso Roman Safiullin en su estreno en el Abierto de Estados Unidos 2026, elevó a 15 la racha victoriosa en partidos de Grand Slam, la mejor secuencia de resultados del tenista murciano en los torneos de máximo valor y que tratará de seguir ampliando el miércoles ante el portugués Jaime Faria en la segunda ronda en Nueva York. Alcaraz acumula 28 partidos resueltos a su favor en sus últimos 29 que disputó en los major. En este periodo perdió sólo la final de Wimbledon 2025 por 6-4, 4-6, 4-6 y 4-6 ante el italiano Jannik Sinner, número uno del fútbol. El pupilo de Samuel López, actualmente tercero en la clasificación ATP, se perdió por lesión, la tenosinovitis que afectó a su muñeca derecha, los torneos de Roland Garros y Wimbledon de este año en lo que a los Grand Slam se refiere y está de vuelta cuatro meses y medio después en el US Open, competición que se llevó tanto el pasado curso como en 2022. El encuentro ganado ante Safiullin se suma a los siete con los que fue campeón en el Abierto de Australia a comienzos del presente ejercicio y a los otros tantos que también ganó en Flushing Meadows hace doce meses. El bagaje del jugador español, de 23 años, es de 92-13 en los 21 torneos de los grandes en cuyos cuadros finales compareció desde que debutó en Melbourne en 2021. Esos guarismos intentará mejorarlos ya este miércoles ante Faria, quien se impuso al estadounidense Jenson Brooksby en cinco sets por 6-3, 7-6 (4), 4-6, 1-6 y 6-2. Será el primer choque entre el español y el luso, también de 23 años y que ocupa el puesto 72 de la clasificación mundial. EFE

articles.title: Thea Frodin played Serena Williams’ body double in ‘King Richard’ at 12; 5 years later, after winning the US junior title that earned her a US Open wild card, she is playing against No. 2 Elena Rybakina
articles.summary: Tennis News: At just 17, Thea Frodin is about to walk onto one of the biggest tennis stages in the world — and her opponent is none other than Elena Rybakina, the .
articles.body: At just 17, Thea Frodin is about to walk onto one of the biggest tennis stages in the world — and her opponent is none other than Elena Rybakina, the No. 2 player in women's tennis.But Frodin isn't exactly a stranger to the spotlight.Before making her U.S. Open singles debut, the Los Angeles teenager had already played Serena Williams on the big screen — sort of.When she was in HollywoodFrodin was the tennis body double for Demi Singleton, who portrayed a young Serena Williams in the 2021 movie “King Richard”, starring Will Smith.The experience took her to a movie set for six months, where she worked alongside major Hollywood actors.“I was on set for six months and I got to be alongside some really cool actors and obviously Will Smith, and just the whole experience was super cool for me,” Frodin said. “And obviously to be able to play the double, or the role of somebody that I look up to and I have always been inspired by was truly, like, a very special experience for me.”But there was one unexpected problem: Frodin became so accustomed to copying Serena's strokes that she struggled to play with her own technique afterward.“It’s actually funny. After I was done with with the movie, I actually got into the habit of using, or playing with her strokes, and I couldn’t switch back to mine because I was so used to hers,” Frodin said. “So my parents — I mean, obviously it’s a great person to replicate — but my parents were a little bit upset because I was playing like Serena, so it took me a while to get back to my normal technique.”She is now in the US OpenNow, Frodin gets to create her own tennis story.“I’ve worked so hard to try and get to this level, and to have an opportunity like this is just really special for me,” Frodin said Monday in a phone interview.Her U.S. Open opportunity came after she won the USTA Billie Jean King Girls’ 18s National Championships and earned a wild card.And while tennis remains her priority, Frodin hasn't ruled out another Hollywood appearance.“Obviously, my No. 1 focus always has been tennis, but I’ve always had this little thought in the back of my mind. I feel like it would be really cool if I could somehow balance both,” Frodin said. “I mean, I loved every second of being in that kind of environment, of that kind of acting life. I enjoy it a lot and yeah, if it’s even possible, I don’t mind having that as a side gig, you know?”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Jaime Faria, de comprarse las raquetas a jugar con Alcaraz siendo el segundo con más victorias este curso
articles.standfirst: El portugués, que explotó hace dos campañas, suma 47 partidos ganados esta temporada
articles.summary: El portugués, que explotó hace dos campañas, suma 47 partidos ganados esta temporada
articles.body: Jaime Faria, el 72 del ranking a sus 23 años, será este miércoles el rival de Carlos Alcaraz por un puesto en la tercera ronda del US Open. A pesar de tener la misma edad, las carreras de ambos no se cruzaron en categorías inferiores. Alcaraz siempre fue uno de los mejores júniors —batiendo récords de precocidad ya entre los profesionales— y Faria fue captado por la federación portuguesa de tenis a los 16 años, cuando estaba en el puesto 106 del ranking sub’18. Fue en los Nacionales de su país. Trasladó su residencia a Oeiras. Todo empezó para él cuando su padre le llevó a un evento del Champions Tour y vio jugar a John McEnroe. Faria dio las primeras señales en 2024 tras ganar cuatro torneos ITF: Vila Real de Santo, Faro, Quinta do Lago y Vale de Lobo. Hasta entonces se compraba las raquetas, de la marca Yonex, y la compañía española Joma le ayudaba con el material deportivo. Tras su victoria en la primera ronda del US Open se convirtió en el portugués más joven en lograr victorias en los cuatro Grand Slam. Y tendrá el premio de medirse al campeón Alcaraz en la majestuosa Arthur Ashe. La pasada campaña ya se enfrentó en la Rod Laver Arena de Melbourne contra Novak Djokovic. Jaime está completando la temporada de su consolidación, con 47 partidos ganados, entre ellos el de Ben Shelton en Cincinnati después de que este se coronara en Montreal. Sólo Rafa Jódar sumó más triunfos, con 49. El portugués ha creado un entorno profesional a su alrededor. Está representado por The Agency, en la figura de David Tosas. Es un gran aficionado al fútbol y seguidor del Sporting de Lisboa.

articles.title: Random Musing: Should Novak Djokovic take a leaf from Lionel Messi and retire?
articles.summary: Tennis News: Exploring the parallels between Novak Djokovic and Lionel Messi, this article questions if Djokovic should retire after his recent performance and what that means for his legacy in tennis.
articles.body: British philosopher Bertrand Russell, the pacifist who was arrested for opposing World War I and spent six months in jail, where he wrote Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy, said: “Conventional people are roused to fury by departure from convention, largely because they regard such departure as a criticism of themselves.”That perhaps explains why Novak Djokovic angers so many people all the time, particularly op-ed columnists. Of course, angering op-ed columnists isn’t a particularly difficult task, as they are wont to lose their nut over a host of things, from a lack of LGBT representation in Harry Potter to “architectural sexism about upward-thrusting buildings ejaculating into the sky”.But one column that lives in this author’s head rent-free was written after Novak Djokovic won his 23rd Grand Slam that argued: “Suppose a tennis player comes along who is 10 feet tall. Every serve is an ace. He never loses a service game. He wins 30 grand slams. Is he the GOAT (greatest of all time)? No. The idea is ridiculous. Or suppose that in the next few years there is another world war, and the majority of young men are conscripted. But the grand slams are still played, and Dave wins 30 of them. Is Dave the greatest? Certainly not.”One doesn’t need to be a Cambridge Don – though they let anyone become one these days if they have fabulist backstories – to decipher why Djokovic has ruffled the feathers of conventional folks.Much like Muhammad Ali, who refused to be drafted during the Vietnam War (“I don’t got no quarrel with the Vietcong”), Djokovic refused to succumb to COVID-era bullying even if it meant passing up history to become the first man to win 20 Grand Slams. He has refused surgery, created a rival players’ organisation, written “Kosovo is the heart of Serbia”, organised a separate tour during the pandemic and challenged equal pay. His father has even been filmed with supporters carrying the Russian flag at the Australian Open, when the polite thing in WENA countries was to pretend that the Russia-Ukraine War was the only global conflict that mattered.And let’s not forget the fact that, despite having the misfortune of being born in the same era as two of tennis’ greatest maestros, Djokovic not only outlasted them but even ensured that the next generation would come up empty when counting their Grand Slam wins. Until his first-round loss at the US Open to the Argentine Mariano Navone, he was the only one who looked capable of challenging the Alcaraz-Sinner duopoly in tennis, despite the fact that those two were born after Djokovic made his professional debut.Such was the dominance of Djokovic, along with Messrs Federer and Nadal, in the noughties and 2010s that only three men born in the 1990s have ever won Majors. The 1990s generation was sadly sandwiched between those born in the 1980s and the Alcaraz-Sinner hegemony that followed in the 2020s, meaning winning became a distant dream unless either protagonist was injured or having a rather bad day.But a recent retirement, in this case that of Lionel Messi, compatriot of Djokovic’s slayer Navone, from international duty, has raised the question of whether Djokovic, too, should consider hanging up his racket.Now, Messi and Djokovic do have a lot in common.Both came from impoverished backgrounds and became the greatest ever to play their respective sports.Both were even born in the same year, just 33 days apart. Both chased dreams that seemed unattainable, with families who bet their futures on their children’s success.Both had similarly close paternal relationships and left home early to train.In their early days, both even faced similar physical limitations. Messi needed growth hormones; Djokovic switched his diet and conditioning to produce extraordinary endurance hitherto unseen in tennis.Both even had to wait until the twilight of their careers for national redemption, with Messi winning the 2021 Copa América and the 2022 World Cup, and Djokovic winning Olympic gold for Serbia in 2024.Even at 39, both remain elite athletes who almost reached greatness again. While Djokovic reached the 2026 Australian Open final after defeating Sinner and falling to Alcaraz, Messi dragged Argentina into the 2026 World Cup final before finally succumbing to a vastly superior Spanish side.In the sign-off note that he was ostensibly going to post on July 21, two days after the final loss, Messi wrote: “I have emptied myself. I have nothing more to give. Besides, there are some wonderful young players coming through who deserve to be here.”Anyone who has watched Messi knows that the boy from Rosario was long tormented by his inability to replicate his club success for the nation of his birth, even after giving it everything.But Novak Djokovic isn’t Lionel Messi, and tennis is not football. Djokovic isn’t taking up some young player’s space or blocking anyone in a team sport, unlike his once-great rival Ronaldo, who has been doing so in the Portuguese national side.There’s no perfect swansong for an ageing GOAT, and if a 22-year-old cannot beat a 39-year-old Djokovic, that’s on the rookie. Djokovic also remains an elite contender, having reached the Australian Open final and, before the US Open, at least the semi-finals in eight of the last 11 majors. It’s only Djokovic’s surreal record that makes it look like a bad innings.Most don’t get perfect swansongs, with Sampras perhaps the only one who left at the top. Federer’s final professional match was a doubles defeat; Nadal’s was a loss in the Davis Cup. Serena Williams lost in the third round of her final US Open.One loss doesn’t tarnish anything Djokovic has achieved in his career, and winning number 25 remains tennis’s Holy Grail. Currently, Djokovic shares 24 Slams with Margaret Court, and the only question is what Djokovic meant by “pretty much despising every moment he spent on court”.He said after the match: “Then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. The back just gave up, in the end it was the shoulder, and I couldn't close it out.”The question here is really one that only Djokovic and his team can answer: Has time taken its toll, or was this a one-off that will see the old Djokovic back on court and joking again? Either way, that first-round loss makes one think of what Winston Churchill said after the British victory at the Second Battle of El Alamein in North Africa: “This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.”One hopes that Djokovic’s first-round loss is not the end of the beginning because, as long as the Serb is around, he will continue to defy conventional wisdom and keep rousing his detractors to fury. And without that tennis will be a far poorer sport.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The tears that might make Novak Djokovic reconsider his tennis future
articles.summary: With tears filling his eyes and his body failing beneath him, you couldn’t help but feel Sunday’s US Open defeat marked a pivotal moment in Novak Djokovic’s career.
articles.body: With tears filling his eyes and his body failing beneath him, you couldn’t help but feel Sunday’s US Open defeat marked a pivotal moment in Novak Djokovic’s career. The first-round defeat to Mariano Navone was not only Djokovic’s worst grand slam result in 20 years, but also one of the few times the Serbian looked vulnerable on a tennis court. His step no longer looked assured, his body appeared stiff and his warrior mentality finally breached. This defeat felt different; it felt more final. It’s important to remember that only seven months ago, the 24-time grand slam champion was playing in the Australian Open final. The 39-year-old was busy defying the odds and seemed the only man capable of laying a glove on the new generation of Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner. Reaching the semifinal at Wimbledon in July also gave Djokovic hope of one day winning that record-breaking 25th major singles title. Now, though, achieving that goal looks as unlikely as ever. In truth, Djokovic is no longer a full-time player on tour. He saves himself for the grand slam tournaments, occasionally using other competitions as warm-ups. This tailored approach has allowed him to manage his body as he’s gotten older, but not even he looks capable of battling against his latest challenge. Earlier this month, the Serb said he had been battling an underlying health issue for a while, something that is exacerbated by playing in hot and humid conditions. That issue raised its head again in his latest defeat, with Djokovic seen vomiting between points and barely being able to move by the end of the match. The tears in the final set were surely a sign that Djokovic felt Father Time was finally catching up with him – that his body was finally unable to keep performing. “I didn’t enjoy myself,” Djokovic said afterward. “I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me.” “It’s something that I’ve been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year: vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there. “Then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. Yeah, the back just gave up in the end and shoulder.” Djokovic left the US Open saying he needed time to think about his future in the sport – whether he could keep putting his body through the pain. After those scenes on Sunday, how could he not be thinking about retirement? But Djokovic has previously said he wants to keep playing until the LA Olympics in 2028, hanging his racket up after representing his country one more time. That dream might look far-fetched to many watching this weekend, but be careful when doubting Djokovic. Time and time again, the veteran has proven people wrong. In 2017, he struggled with an elbow injury and some wondered if he would ever return to his best. In 2018, he won two out of the four grand slams. In recent seasons, the retirement narrative has followed him around like a bad spell. Every start of a new year is supposedly the beginning of the end for him as a player, every defeat seen as the last opportunity to clinch another major trophy. But Djokovic has continued to plug away, seemingly adapting his game as he ages and rolling back the years to win matches that silence the critics – notably a five-set thriller against Sinner at the Australian Open at the start of the year. But the truth is that Djokovic hasn’t won a grand slam title since 2023 and that should be a surprise to absolutely no one. The Serb’s once-great rivals Roger Federer and Rafa Nadal both won their last majors at 36, and the demands of the game are now so physical that Djokovic would need a lot of fortune if he’s ever going to challenge the new generation again. So while his painful defeat on Sunday might prove to be yet another false flag, it’s surely more likely that it’s finally the beginning of the end for him. The expression on his face as he tried to muster up some sort of challenge certainly made it feel that way. Djokovic has always been in control on court, a master of his surroundings. This time, he looked defeated and maybe he realized that too for the first time. Whatever happens in the next few months, Djokovic will still go down as arguably the greatest tennis player in history and he won’t be the last champion to hold onto the sport for a touch too long. Perhaps reframing what he defines as success would help him continue for another year or two, but whether the champion would be happy with that is another question entirely.

articles.title: ‘I felt great’: Carlos Alcaraz makes stunning US Open return after 139 days out with wrist injury
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: For two hours and 21-minutes on Arthur Ashe, Carlos Alcaraz’s game answered the big question that had accompanied his much-anticipated .
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: For two hours and 21-minutes on Arthur Ashe, Carlos Alcaraz’s game answered the big question that had accompanied his much-anticipated return to tennis.The 23-year-old Spaniard, playing his first match in 139 days after a wrist injury in mid-April, faced Russia’s Roman Safiullin in the US Open. He pummelled the ball, pulled off impossible gets and picked up shots off his shoelaces, turning defence into delicate winners on his way to a convincing 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 win.Alcaraz opened his final service game with a volley winner, caressed inches above the ground, then turned to the crowd, calling for some love, hand on his ear. The spectators roared and Alcaraz’ smile sparked the sun.The second seed underlined that he was playing pain-free.“I felt great. I don’t know how it looked from outside, but from inside, my feeling was that I was hitting the ball normal. I was playing pretty normal, playing my style, and the wrist felt great. I'm going to still take care of it, obviously, I'm just really happy it's pain-free finally,” he told international media.The defending champion arrived on court in a dark-brown, almost espresso, ensemble, the fashion world’s warmer alternative to black. Alcaraz shed his overshirt to reveal an oversized ombré sleeveless tank, paired with matching brown shorts edged in a thick white trim. A narrow hairband held his unruly mop in place. A white compression sleeve covered the precautionary taping on his wrist.In a match of small margins, where Alcaraz, it appeared was doing just enough, he hit 28 winners, 20 of them off the forehand. He faced six breakpoints, with Safiullin converting just one. The 23-year-old converted four of the seven break points he earned, a difference that proved decisive.The second seed teed off on his returns, but was more controlled with his serve. Alcaraz, who enjoys amping up the speed upwards of 130 mph, hit a top speed of 128 in the first-round match. The average speed on his first and second serves was 113 and 97 respectively.“The serve is the shot that I was struggling the most,” he said, adding, “There are some players who like to return serves coming at 130 miles and when you serve a little bit slower they struggle a little bit. So most of that speed (generated) is because of him (opponent). It was kind of tactics.”“I just always struggle with the serve, but it will be back, for sure,” he said.For the seven-time major winner, who faces 23-year-old Jaime Faria of Portugal in the second round on Tuesday, the biggest shift was perhaps mental.“It was a difficult day for me, but at the same time, a really beautiful day,” he said. “I was really nervous. Really, really nervous, but also just happy, because, for me, my goal here is to compete, to enjoy, and let's see how my body's going to react after the matches.”Alcaraz explained, “I had forgotten how a match day feels like. I was warming up, and I don't remember actually what I used to do, in the warm-up. So to kind of get that feeling again. That's why I was really nervous, because kind of I just forgot the competition.”“I don't know how far I'm going to go in the tournament,” he admitted, “But what I just really want to do is enjoy every time that I'm going to walk into the court, feeling the energy from the people, feeling the competition. That's why I enjoyed so much today.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Aryna Sabalenka Continues To Hint at Tensions With Tennis Community With Blunt Replies and ‘Haters’ Remark at US Open
articles.summary: Aryna Sabalenka kicked off her 2026 US Open title defense with a commanding 6-2, 6-4 victory over Colombia’s Camila Osorio. However, the top seed’s on-court...
articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka kicked off her 2026 US Open title defense with a commanding 6-2, 6-4 victory over Colombia's Camila Osorio. However, the top seed's on-court performance has had to share the spotlight with intense scrutiny from all sides, amid questions about the recent dip in form, her busy off-court lifestyle, and her polarizing fashion choices.

Aryna Sabalenka Addresses Critics and Media Pressure After Winning US Open Opener

Sabalenka's season got off to a strong start after reaching the Australian Open final and completing the Sunshine Double with titles in Indian Wells and Miami. However, her momentum slowed as the tour moved to clay.

She has now gone seven tournaments without reaching a final, including fourth-round exits at Wimbledon, the Canadian Open, and the Cincinnati Open. As a result, her World No. 1 ranking is under threat from Elena Rybakina, Coco Gauff, and Jessica Pegula. To remain at the top, Sabalenka must win a third consecutive US Open title.

The pressure was evident during her pre-tournament press conference. When a reporter pointed to her frustration in Cincinnati and asked whether there was "anything wrong" with her game, the 28-year-old responded sharply: "Maybe there's something wrong with people."

After her first-round win against Osorio, when a journalist questioned whether her packed schedule of off-court events could affect her performance, Sabalenka shut down the idea that her brand commitments were a distraction.

"It's like my hobby outside of tennis," Sabalenka said. "The whole schedule we plan is all around tennis. So all of those events are not drawing me in any way. And all the people that I work with, all the brands that I work with, I choose them very carefully. I have to be really comfortable around those people, just so in that case, I'm not drawing my energy when I'm surrounded by them.

"So I'm really enjoying my time with my brands, with people who work there, and I have fun. It's like my hobby outside of my tennis schedule, and it actually gives me so much energy," said the Belarusian.

It was not just Sabalenka's recent results and off-court brand events that drew criticism. Her Nike US Open outfit, a black mesh dress over a bright orange sports bra and shorts, also drew significant backlash from fans who believe it's inappropriate and not suitable for the four-time Grand Slam champion.

Her custom 127-carat "Silhouette Suite" jewelry from Material Good, which she wears on court, also drew mixed reactions. The outfit and jewelry became topics of discussion during her pressers in New York.

In her post-match talk with Sky Sports, Sabalenka made it clear that she no longer wants to pay attention to the outside noise.

"Honestly, it took me a little while to shut down those noises," she said . "I'm so tired of those miserable haters. Whoever loves me, they're going to be there for me no matter what. Haters, honestly, I don't want to curse here right now, but they can go and have fun with their own lives."

While Sabalenka continues to face criticism from fans and the media, she remains focused on her US Open campaign. The World No. 1 will face 22-year-old Russian qualifier Polina Iatcenko in the second round.

articles.title: What to Know About Thea Frodin, Serena Williams' Former Movie Body Double Making US Open Debut At 17
articles.summary: Thea Frodin is making her U.S. Open debut against No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina in the first round on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Thea Frodin is making her U.S. Open debut against No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina in the first round on Tuesday.

Frodin served as the tennis-playing body double for actress Demi Singleton, who played a young Serena Williams in the 2021 film, King Richard .

That movie starred Will Smith as Richard Williams, the father of Serena and Venus Williams, as he navigated many trials and tribulations en route to charting his daughters' early paths to tennis superstardom.

"It helps that I was kind of playing a sport that I've done my whole life, so it didn't feel too new," Frodin said, per Richard Osborn of the US Open website.

"I just had to go out and play tennis, try to replicate her strokes a little bit. Doing it with [Richard Williams portrayer] Will Smith was super cool. He's a super nice guy. He actually gave me some on-set tips and things to take with me."

Frodin has enjoyed great success on the junior circuit and notably reached the semifinals of the girls' singles draw at the 2026 Australian Open.

She's also done well in junior doubles, making the quarterfinals of the Australian Open and Roland-Garros this year. Frodin reached the junior doubles finals at Wimbledon in 2025.

She's now making her debut on the main major stage after winning the USTA Billie Jean King Girls' 18s National Championships , which earned her a wild card spot.

Frodin is also hoping to meet the Williams sisters, who are playing doubles as a wild card, while in New York.

"Hopefully, if I get a chance to hit with them or just meet them, anything, I'll take it," Frodin said, per Osborn. "That would be incredible. That would be a dream."

In the meantime, Frodin is enjoying fantastic success herself after a tremendous run landed her on one of tennis' greatest stages.

articles.title: Allen Iverson Reacts to Naomi Osaka Honoring NBA Icon With US Open Outfit in Trending Video, Photos
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka's tribute to Allen Iverson caught the attention of the NBA legend.
articles.body:
Naomi Osaka's tribute to Allen Iverson caught the attention of the NBA legend.

"Wow, what a honor!! BIG FAN can't wait to meet you. @naomiosaka" he wrote on Instagram.

While warming up prior to her first-round victory over Anastasia Zakharova at the U.S. Open, Osaka donned a shooting sleeve, headband and elbow pad to mimic Iverson's on-court look.

Serena's stunt double playing in US Open

Osaka also wore a T-shirt showcasing Iverson's iconic Slam Magazine cover from 1999 while speaking to reporters leading up to the match. She described the Hall of Fame guard as a "trailblazer."

"I think he's also someone that I look up to a lot, because he's kind of like done a lot in fashion, whether it's on purpose or not, but he's shifted the way that NBA players dress," she said. "I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports and also just expressing yourself through style, I feel like he's someone that I look up to in that regard."

Iverson is generally credited with playing a role in the NBA's implementation of a stricter dress code in 2005. He embraced an everyday style when he arrived to the arena until commissioner David Stern required players to go more business casual.

Far predating Osaka, a generation of young ballers adopted Iverson's headband and shooting sleeve when they took the court. The sleeve initially served a medical purpose as Iverson was dealing with an elbow issue. Over time, he decided to keep wearing it anyway.

Perhaps the homage brought Osaka some good luck. She took down Zakharova in straight sets.

The two-time U.S. Open champion will meet Katerina Siniakova in the second round.

articles.summary: La kazaja debuta con victoria en el US Open ante Thea Frodin y pone su mira en la cima del mundo
articles.body: Elena Rybakina tiene un objetivo claro en Nueva York. La actual número dos del ranking ha superado su debut ante la americana, e intérprete de la menor de las Williams en la película 'El método Williams', Thea Frodin (585 del mundo) por 6-3 y 6-2 y está a cinco partidos (tiene que alcanzar las semifinales) de destronar a Aryna Sabalenka y convertirse en la nueva reina de la WTA. Ha sido un partido cómodo para la kazaja. En una hora y 15 minutos ya firmaba su primera victoria sobre las pistas de Flushing Meadows y la octava seguida en pista dura en torneos de Grand Slam. Encadenada con las siete que logró en Australia a principios de año que le dieron el título en Melbourne. Son 17 los golpes ganadores que ha sumado ante su rival, 10 años menor que ella. Aunque en todo momento ha querido mostrar la importancia de la evolución de las molestias en el talón de Aquiles que la obligaron a retirarse en los cuartos de final de Cincinnati: "Lo veremos día a día. articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina makes winning start in race to world number one
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina says she is "motivated" by the race to become world number one but is simply taking things "day by day" after getting her US Open campaign off to a winning start.
articles.body:
Elena Rybakina says she is "motivated" by the race to become world number one but is simply taking things "day by day" after getting her US Open campaign off to a winning start.

Playing for the first time since withdrawing midway through her Cincinnati Masters quarter-final with a heel injury last month, Rybakina showed no signs of discomfort as she eased to a dominant 6-3 6-2 win over 17-year-old wildcard Thea Frodin.

The 27-year-old second seed trails Aryna Sabalenka by just 434 points in the world rankings and will become number one for the first time by reaching the semi-finals in New York – even if Sabalenka defends her title.

Regardless of her performance, Rybakina will also secure the top ranking if none of Sabalenka, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula lift the trophy.

"I'm definitely motivated [to become world number one]," said Rybakina, who trailed Sabalenka by more than 3,000 points in the spring before the Belarusian entered a mid-season slump.

"I feel like I had opportunities before and it didn't go my way. It will be an amazing achievement but it's still too far and I need to focus on my day off tomorrow, my recovery, and just keep on going."

Fighting to stay No 1 - Sabalenka's US Open mission

Sabalenka wins to begin bid for US Open 'three-peat'

Rybakina, a two-time Grand Slam winner, arrived at Flushing Meadows with question marks around her fitness after retiring injured against Iga Swiatek in Cincinnati.

Though she looked comfortable on court, her movement went largely untested by Frodin - who acted as Serena Williams' body double in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard' - as she blew the world number 585 away on serve and dictated points from the baseline.

"We didn't know if [I was] going to be able to play here or not. I'm pretty happy that I'm playing right now, and we are taking [it] day by day," Rybakina said about her injury.

"I was not playing for the full week [before the tournament], so seven days no tennis and basically not too much gym I could do movement-wise.

"So it's a great result after 10 days from that kind of injury."

After opening the rain-delayed match with a double fault, Rybakina proved relentless on serve, dropping just three points and reeling off three consecutive love holds in the first set.

She didn't face a break point until the sixth game of the second set, saving both.

Equally clinical in Frodin's service games, she converted her first three break points to race into a set and 5-1 lead.

However, the young wildcard, making her WTA Tour main-draw debut after winning the United States Tennis Association (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championship, made Rybakina work to get over the line, saving three match points with aces in her final service game among 11 across the match.

Rybakina served out the win with an ace of her own – her sixth of the match and a tour-leading 363rd of the season.

"She played really well today. She has great shots, great serve, it was no easy," Rybakina said of the largely unknown Frodin.

Serena Williams meets Wimbledon opponent in women's doubles

Serena Williams is set for a rematch with Maya Joint, who beat the American great in three sets on her singles return at Wimbledon in June, in the women's doubles.

Williams, partnering her sister Venus at a Grand Slam for the first time since 2022, has been drawn against Australian Joint and Chan Hao-chingof Taiwan.

The Williams sisters, who were awarded a wildcard to compete in New York, won 14 double titles together between 1999 and 2016, including two US Opens.

They were due to renew their partnership at Wimbledon but Serena picked up a knee injury in her 6-3 6-7 (6-8) 6-3 first-round defeat by Joint.

articles.title: Welcome to the US Open. Please bring your wallet
articles.summary: The U.S. Open has beceom a bucket-list event. But at what cost?
articles.body:
NEW YORK — At some point within the past handful of years, the US Open joined the Masters and the Kentucky Derby in the elite tier of sporting events that many Americans, whether they care about the sport or not, want to cross off their bucket list.

In the era of social media, this was probably unavoidable. For as long as the tournament has been here at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, it has been as much about the sensory festival that takes place outside the courts as the tennis itself.

Everything here is designed to catch the eye. From the red carpet area where celebrities arrive to the luxury brands that set up stores around the perimeter of the show courts to the pink hue of the Honey Deuce — the tournament's signature cocktail — it's all optimized to signal that you're part of an exclusive experience that transcends the mundane, even old-fashioned act of attending a sporting event to watch sports.

What was once a very New York-coded event — Wall Street corporate types and entertainers filling the expensive seats in Arthur Ashe Stadium, the local loudmouths drinking late into the night and creating the most daunting atmosphere in tennis — has become a tableau to fill your Instagram feed with images of a lifestyle you can only get by coming here.

"Every Slam has their own identity, and the US Open has always been the big show Grand Slam," said Madison Keys, who is playing here for the 15th time. "You can see (now) there's a lot more, like, influencers."

For its part, the US Open is leaning all the way into its newfound cultural cachet. It has created a separate credential for content creators in hopes of selling the experience of attending a tennis tournament to a younger, wider demographic. Craig Tiley, who was hired away from Tennis Australia to run the U.S. Tennis Association earlier this year, said he envisions the US Open becoming "the tennis Disneyland."

But the tradeoffs of straying from the core tennis audience — and the USTA's chase to extract every possible dollar out of this event — have begun to emerge as a hot topic.

In the days leading up to the event, ticket prices on the secondary market surged to more than $300 for a grounds pass that retails for $65. Fan Week, which takes place around qualifying the week before the main draw and offers free access to the grounds, has gotten so big that you now have to register for a pass to prevent overcrowding. Over the first couple days of the main draw, it was common to see long lines of people trying to get into the outer courts, where seating is first-come, first-serve. And even if you can get in the door, there is no break from captive capitalism at the concession stands where you'll pay $30 for a Carnegie Deli-branded hot pastrami sandwich, $23 for the Honey Deuce and $42 for a glass of the Moët & Chandon Nectar Imperial Rosé.

For older fans who remember a simpler (and cheaper) time at this tournament, it might bring to mind the classic Yogi Berra line about Ruggeri's restaurant in St. Louis: "Nobody goes there anymore — it's too crowded." But actually the opposite is true. As demand continues to spike, there seems to be no end to how much money the USTA can squeeze out of these three weeks, even if fans have to endure a longer line or two and reach deeper into their pockets to get through the gates.

"I think it's a nice problem, I guess you could say, because there is an insatiable appetite to come out to Flushing and to watch all the opportunities we have for the fans," Tiley said. "One of the things we need to be very conscious of is getting the balance of how well we manage that. It will be something that we'll continue to make sure that we stay on top of. We're not going to be one of those events that just want to pack the precinct for the sake of packing it."

As the US Open continues down this path, however, it will face increased scrutiny about whether its purpose has become out of line with its ambitions.

On Monday, the USTA announced a "groundbreaking partnership" with Kalshi to be the first "Official prediction market" of the US Open, which is an odd look for a sport where players receive tremendous amounts of online abuse from gamblers and match fixing has been a longstanding problem at the sport's lower levels.

Meanwhile, the tournament is being played in the midst of a two-year, $800 million renovation of Arthur Ashe Stadium that focuses on adding premium (i.e., more expensive) seating and luxury suites rather than additional access for the common fan.

And all this for a nonprofit organization whose mission statement is "Growing tennis to inspire healthier people and communities everywhere."

In many ways, the completion of the Ashe renovations will bring the US Open full circle. When the tournament moved in 1978 from the small but elite West Side Tennis Club on the other side of Queens to this new public facility with a huge stadium, it brought tennis out of American country club culture to the masses for the first time.

Now, it's just like every other premium sports experience in this country: Unaffordable for most, more popular than ever and the ultimate stage for players to market themselves and their sponsors.

"Even if you're not a quote-unquote 'tennis fan,' people know about the US Open," said three-time Grand Slam doubles champion Taylor Townsend, who is using the tournament to debut custom outfits she designed with a celebrity stylist. "I think there's a super cool intersection between culture and sports across the board and we're in a fun and entertaining time. I'm honored to be someone that is pushing culture forward, to inspire people, to carry the torch for representation and having a completely different brand identity than any other outlet out here and doing things in a unique way. So the US Open kind of gives me the runway to be able to do that because of what it means for everyone."

This is all, of course, great for the players who see their faces plastered on billboards all over New York and mingle with the city's elite at various sponsor events in the week leading up to the tournament. Also, prize money this year will be a record $108 million, with $5.5 million each to the men's and women's singles champion. Even a first-round loss in the singles main draw is worth $140,000.

The tournament's largesse has minted a lot of financial winners including the USTA, which makes 90 percent of its annual revenue (more than $600 million) off the event. But it has changed the tournament in ways that seem hard to dial back.

As a response to the ticket price discourse, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani managed last week to negotiate for 1,000 tickets to be sold at $100 each only to New Yorkers via an online lottery. More than 300,000 people registered in hopes of landing one.

As much as accessibility is a worthy goal, it's not possible to engineer it in a way that satisfies everyone. That's supply-and-demand at work. At the same time, letting the secondary ticket market rip to the point where it costs more than $300 to get in the door feels discordant with the mission of an organization whose goal is supposed to be growing interest in tennis.

"One thing that's critically important to us as an event is we want kids to be able to experience, there's the sense or having the aspiration of wanting to become a player in their future lives when they get to see the players of today," Tiley said. "We need to continue to find ways to make it affordable, and most importantly, accessible. The US Open, as a sporting and entertainment event, is up there, No. 1 or No. 2 in the United States and potentially globally, and that demand is something we have to match with the balance of making sure kids have access."

That's going to become harder and harder if the tournament and its influencer army continues to make this a bucket list experience for more people. Contrast that with the Masters, which has chosen (for the most part) to keep its vibe bespoke and its prices low by controlling its ticket supply through a lottery and strictly prohibiting resales.

It's great for those who are lucky enough to get tickets. It's agony for those who apply for the lottery year after year and continually get shut out, even if they have the means to attend.

Is an experience that can't be bought on the secondary market better than an event like this where anyone can buy their way in? That's in the eye of the beholder (or, more to the point, the ticket holder). But no matter the price or the inconvenience, people still can't get enough. If there's a limit to what people will pay to see Grand Slam tennis, the US Open has not yet rubbed up against it.

"Every year I come here, I'm like, 'Wow, it's pretty insane,'" said 46th-ranked Alex Michelsen. "There are so many people, but I love it."

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Arthur Fery's debut ended by Lorenzo Musetti in first round
articles.summary: Arthur Fery is unable to produce a repeat of his Wimbledon heroics as his US Open debut ends in a first-round loss to Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.
articles.body:
Arthur Fery was unable to produce a repeat of his Wimbledon heroics as his US Open debut ended in a first-round defeat by Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.

Fery, 24, was seeking to build on a sensational, breakout run to the semi-finals at his home Grand Slam this summer, an achievement which catapulted him from 114th in the rankings to inside the top 40.

But having narrowly missed out on a seeded position in New York - awarded to the top 32 players - the world number 33 was unfortunate to draw talented all-rounder Musetti in his opener.

Musetti, a quarter-finalist 12 months ago but absent from the past two majors because of a thigh injury, spoiled Fery's hopes of launching a revival by immediately breaking back twice in the third set before completing a 6-3 6-3 7-5 victory.

This was only British number one Fery's second appearance at an overseas major, following his maiden Australian Open campaign in January.

He was made to wait longer than he might have anticipated to make his tournament bow on a rain-delayed third day at Flushing Meadows, and the match was eventually contested in hot and humid conditions.

Full of confidence after producing one of the great British stories of recent years at Wimbledon, and off the back of reaching his first ATP Tour final at the Winston-Salem Open, Fery appeared at home on Grandstand - the US Open's third-biggest arena.

The Briton wore ear plugs during each change of ends, just as he did at Wimbledon to maintain his focus and block out any distracting noise.

But Musetti proved a silent assassin here, biding his time and making few mistakes when the opportunities arrived.

Recap US Open: GB's Fery beaten in straight sets on debut by Musetti

Musetti has described his versatile game as "vintage", not least because of his impressive, trademark one-handed backhand which repeatedly hurt Fery.

But the Briton delighted with his inventive play during the two-hour contest, and caused Musetti headaches with his early effectiveness at the net in particular.

However, despite a promising start, Fery gifted his opponent the breakthrough with back-to-back double faults, before losing serve again to concede the first set.

It was with a sublime backhand winner that Musetti took charge of the second set on his first break point opportunity, before withstanding four break points to hold for a 5-2 lead.

Refusing to lose hope after falling two sets down, Fery threatened to launch a fightback in the third when he broke for the first time to take a 2-0 lead.

That revival was short-lived. Musetti produced an immediate response, embarking on a four-game run as the errors began creeping in for the fading Fery.

While Fery refused to yield when faced with a first match point on his serve, and kept the crowd engaged by breaking back to level at five games apiece, he was again left frustrated by his inability to back it up.

Musetti pointed to his head in celebration after eventually seizing his third match point and setting up a second-round meeting with Australian Dane Sweeny.

While disappointed to exit at the first hurdle, this invaluable experience will not take away from a memorable year for Fery, who remained outside the world's top 200 12 months ago.

The first men's wildcard to reach the last four at Wimbledon for 25 years, he will look to push on in 2027 after establishing himself in the upper echelons of the game.

Fery, who had never progressed beyond the second round at one of the sport's major tournaments before this summer, has already hinted that will be the case after going close to his first ATP title in North Carolina on Saturday.

The task of repeating his spectacular Wimbledon run always appeared a tall one following the draw in New York, and British interest in the men's singles now rests with Jacob Fearnley, Toby Samuel and Jan Choinski, who plays later on Tuesday.

articles.title: US Open: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams body double from 'King Richard,' falls to No. 2 Elena Rybakina in Grand Slam debut
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina began her quest for the No. 1 ranking against an interesting opponent.
articles.body:
Serena Williams did not enter the singles draw for the 2026 US Open. That doesn't mean she didn't have a presence in the background.

Years ago, Thea Frodin performed as a body double for actor Demi Singleton's performance as Williams in the Academy Award-winning movie "King Richard." Now 17 years old, she made her Grand Slam singles debut on Tuesday, as the first-round opponent for No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina.

Rybakina won 6-3, 6-2, but it was still a special moment in Frodin's young career.

Per the Associated Press , Frodin was invited to audition for the Williams role after she won the singles, doubles and mixed doubles sectional titles at the 10-and-under level in California.

Frodin, a lifelong Williams fan, wound up getting the on-court responsibilities and doing the job for six months:

"I was on set for six months and I got to be alongside some really cool actors and obviously Will Smith, and just the whole experience was super cool for me," Frodin said. "And obviously to be able to play the double, or the role of somebody that I look up to and I have always been inspired by was truly, like, a very special experience for me."

Frodin, who reportedly never met Serena or Venus Williams, continued to compete following the movie and won the USTA Billie Jean King Girls' 18s National Championships this year, earning her a wild card into the singles draw this year. She also competed in doubles at the US Open last year alongside fellow teenager Kristina Penickova.

Rybakina was obviously a tough first test. Frodin actually posted more aces than the big-serving Kazakh (11-6), but the difference in level was clear on second serve, with Rybakina winning 20 of 25 (80%) of those points in her service games, compared Frodin's 11 of 32 (34.4%). Frodin showed off impressive power, but Rybakina was simply steadier from the baseline.

Rybakina was impressed in her post-match interview:

"She played really well today. She has great shots, great serve. It was not easy. I'm just happy to be here, playing here. Thank you so much for coming and supporting us. It's always a nice atmosphere. I really enjoyed it."

The match was one of the most-anticipated of the first round. All eyes will remain on Rybakina going forward as well.

Elena Rybakina is on the verge of WTA's No. 1 ranking

Rybakina is so close to grabbing the top WTA ranking from No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka that she technically didn't even need to beat Frodin to make it possible .

Because Sabalenka is defending her 2,000 rankings points from her US Open title last year, while Rybakina only has 240 points to defend, Rybakina would need some very specific things to happen to remain No. 2. Here's how the scenarios play out:

Rybakina reaches semifinal : Rybakina becomes No. 1 no matter what.

Rybakina does not reach semifinal, one of Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula or Coco Gauff wins the title : The champion is No. 1.

Rybakina does not reach semifinal, none of Sabalenka, Pegula or Gauff win the title: Rybakina becomes No. 1 no matter what.

With the win over Frodin, Rybakina is now four wins from reaching the semifinal, with No. 8 seed Iga Swiatek and No. 13 seed Naomi Osaka representing her most dangerous potential opponents in the quarterfinals.

The bigger concern might be Rybakina's health, as she had to retire against Swiatek in Cincinnati with what turned out to be a heel injury . That injury didn't hobble her too much Tuesday, but she noted that her recovery will be worth monitoring:

"We'll see day by day. I'm glad I played the match, I won the match. We'll see how I feel tomorrow.. Because I had to take quite a break. I wasn't playing or doing much physically. For me now a step at a time. The most important is to recover and listen to the body. For now it's been okay."

Rybakina's second-round opponent will be the winner of the match between Darja Vidmanova and Jessica Bouzas Maneiro, which was suspended due to rain with Bouzas leading 6-3, 3-2.

Maria Sakkari recovered from 6-2, 4-0 down to beat Robin Montgomery 2-6, 7-5, 6-2, while fifth-seeded Flavio Cobolli fought back from two sets down to defeat Francisco Comesana after more than four hours."Just kept telling myself that everything is possible and just try to get myself in a good place mentally and just try to be a little bit more positive, try to make more balls, get myself into the match," Sakkari said. "Because, I mean, everyone's very good in tennis nowadays, but specifically that girl I played today doesn't have the experience that I do. So I just told myself, let's try and hang in there, try and make more balls, and it worked."Cobolli summed up the Grand Slam mentality simply: "In Grand Slams it's never done. articles.title: Serena, Venus Williams' US Open Doubles 1st-Round Opponent Revealed After Women's Draw
articles.summary: Serena Williams will have an opportunity to avenge her Wimbledon defeat to Maya Joint, albeit in a different format.
articles.body:
Serena Williams will have an opportunity to avenge her Wimbledon defeat to Maya Joint, albeit in a different format.

Serena and sister Venus were drawn against Joint and Hao-Ching Chan in the opening round of the women's doubles tournament at the U.S. Open.

Serena and Venus are coming off a loss to Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns in the first round of the women's doubles tournament at the Cincinnati Open. It was their first match together since the 2022 U.S. Open. An injury to Serena prevented them from competing at Wimbledon.

Serena Williams' stunt double to make US Open debut

"I think we give each other so much grace and encouragement," Venus said at the Cincinnati Open. "This is our first time playing together in forever, and I think we're really getting our stride for sure so that was great for us to get out there and do it."

Serena also teamed with Carlos Alcaraz in the U.S. Open mixed doubles event. They defeated Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool before losing to Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli in the quarterfinals.

As accomplished as they are as singles players, the Williams sisters were just as good in doubles at their peak. They've combined for 14 Grand Slam titles, two of which came in the U.S. Open.

Joint and Chan will be a tough test out of the gate. The pair advanced to the quarterfinals of the Cincinnati Open and reached the final of the Memphis Classic earlier this year.

Chan is an experienced doubles player, getting to the semifinals of the 2024 U.S. Open with Veronika Kudermetova. The 32-year-old was also a runner-up in women's doubles at Wimbledon in 2017.

articles.title: US Open: Coco Gauff makes storming start while Serena and Venus Williams are drawn to face Maya Joint and Chan Hao-Ching  in women's doubles
articles.summary: Coco Gauff makes winning start with Williams sisters to begin US Open women's doubles against team with Maya Joint, who beat Serena in singles at Wimbledon; Alexander Zverev rallied to avoid a first round loss; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+
articles.body:
Home favourite Gauff arrived ‌fresh from winning the Cincinnati Open and is chasing a third Grand Slam title ​after her breakthrough triumph in New York in 2023.

The American, who ​has reached the fourth round or better here ​in each of the last four years, will face either Daria Kasatkina or Paula Badosa in the second ‌round.

"I wasn't that nervous today, which was a shock," Gauff said ​on court. "When I walked back out on this court, ‌I was trying to hold back a smile."

Gauff was in control early as she took the only break of serve in the first set and wrapping up the opener in just over ​half an hour.

World No 53 Sonmez showed flashes of ⁠her talent and produced a string ⁠of impressive winners, including a blistering backhand that drew applause from the crowd on Arthur Ashe Stadium and even Gauff herself.

Sonmez, 24, ‌settled in the second set, trading breaks, and began testing the American with deep ‌groundstrokes and forays to the net.

Gauff came under pressure trailing 3-2 but fought off three break points to hold and level the set before breaking Sonmez to reassert control at 4-3.

The 22-year-old pulled away from there as Sonmez ⁠struggled to sustain the level that had briefly unsettled ​the fourth seed, leaving Gauff to close out a comfortable win.

"I know that I can raise my level if ​I need to," said Gauff. "I like to challenge my opponent to ⁠keep up that level the whole match, and if they do, I clap my hands and walk off the court with my head held high. But ⁠I was able to settle down."

Serena to face Wimbledon rematch with Maya Joint - but in women's doubles!

Serena and Venus Williams will compete together in the women's doubles againstthe team of Hao-Ching Chan and Maya Joint - who beat Serena at Wimbledon this summer.

The Americans, who won the US Open doubles title in 1999 and 2009, last played together at a Grand Slam in New York in 2022, losing in the first round.

The sisters planned to reunite at Wimbledon following Serena's return to competition during the grass-court season in June, but she withdrew after suffering a knee injury in her first-round singles match against Maya Joint.

Serena, 44, returned this year after four years out of action and lost to Joint, a 20-year-old from Australia.

She injured her knee in the match and had to pull out of her planned doubles match at the All England Club with Venus, 46.

The teamed up at the Western & Southern Open in Cincinnati, where they lost in the first round to Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

Joint and Chan are the No 14-seeded team.

The first round of the women's doubles tournament begins Thursday.

No Hollywood ending for body double Frodin

Second seed Elena Rybakina also advanced after beating teenage American wild card Thea Frodin 6-3 6-2.

Frodin once played Serena Williams' double in the tennis scenes during the Oscar-winning film about the lives of Serena and her sister Venus, King Richard, starring Will Smith.

She said: "I actually have not met her yet. But hopefully I can get the chance soon to get the opportunity to meet her. "I saw that Will Smith reposted one of my posts, so that was pretty cool and a cool experience."#

Top-seeded Alexander Zverev rallies just in time to avoid a first-round exit

In the men's draw, Alexander Zverev rallied just in time to avoid becoming the first men's No 1 seed to lose in the first round of a Grand Slam tournament since 2003, edging Lorenzo Sonego 6-4, 3-6, 6-7 (7), 7-5, 6-4 in a match that ended in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Zverev won his first major title at the French Open, lost to top-ranked Jannik Sinner in the Wimbledon final, then became the No 1 seed in a major for the first time when Sinner had to withdraw with a right knee injury.

He couldn't cash in on repeated chances to break Sonego's serve for much of the night and was in danger of becoming the first top-seeded man to fall in his first match in a major since Ivo Karlovic beat Lleyton Hewitt at Wimbledon in 2003.

It hasn't happened at the US Open since Stefan Edberg lost to Alexander Volkov in 1990. Zverev finally broke through against Sonego's serve late to pull out the match in 4 hours, 52 minutes.

Fifth seed Flavio Cobolli needed five sets to see off Argentinian Francisco Comesana, while ninth seed Taylor Fritz - one of the big hopes for a home success in New York this year - beat fellow American Darwin Blanch in three.

Frenchman Gael Monfils , who retires at the end of the year, celebrated his 40th birthday in style with a 2-6 6-2 6-1 6-0 victory over Adolfo Alvarez.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Coco Gauff shows rejuvenated serve is a weapon in win over Zeynep Sonmez
articles.summary: At last year's US Open, Coco Gauff's serve left her practising in the rain and crying on court - now it is a potent weapon.
articles.body:
The sight of a forlorn Coco Gauff hitting serves in the rain on the US Open practice courts became the defining image of her struggles last year.

The serving yips were undermining the two-time major champion's talent. Staying out in the persistent drizzle was a sign of how desperate she had become to iron out the major flaw in her game.

Twelve months on, the 22-year-old American has returned to the US Open with a rejuvenated service game - and it was the bedrock of her 6-3 6-4 win over Turkey's Zeynep Sonmez in the New York first round on Tuesday.

Gauff starting with a swift hold to love set the tone for a dominant first set, then used her opening shot to get her out of trouble when Sonmez threatened to go a break up in the second set.

"Now it's like I can look back a year on and think, 'Oh, wow, it's a big difference'," said Gauff, who is seeded fourth at Flushing Meadows this year.

"It feels good to come into a tournament feeling confident on that shot finally."

No repeat of Wimbledon heroics as Fery exits US Open

Rybakina makes winning start in race to number one

On the eve of her home Slam last year, Gauff decided to reshuffle her coaching team and hired biomechanics expert Gavin MacMillan - who helped four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka overcome serving troubles earlier in her career.

It was a drastic move. But one which Gauff felt was unavoidable after hitting a high amount of double faults at the preceding Cincinnati Open.

Tweaking technique heading into the US Open - where she receives frenzied attention - was always going to be a risk.

So it was no surprise when Gauff suffered a fourth-round exit in a tournament where she looked fraught throughout and was reduced to tears during matches.

"Obviously last year I knew all the eyes were going to be on the serve," Gauff said.

"Gavin is so great at what he does, I felt a lot of pressure to kind of prove that. It didn't really show within the first two weeks, which is normal."

That was then. Now Gauff possesses a serve which is a serious weapon - even though she still leaks some double faults.

Showing greater consistency on the toss, not throwing the ball too far in front and keeping her wrist straighter have been MacMillan's pointers for a more reliable serve.

It was a key factor in her charge to the Cincinnati Open title earlier this month.

Analysis from that tournament showed how Gauff is hitting closer to the line but still maintaining her serve speed - underlining a significant improvement in her accuracy.

Gauff now has full confidence her serve can be too hot for opponents to handle - and it showed immediately against Sonmez.

The opening game saw Gauff thump a 112mph ace down the middle, followed by an unreturned first serve and another ace, on her way to holding serve in less than 90 seconds.

Sonmez struggled to get balls into play whenever Gauff landed a first serve in the first set, with the world number four winning 93% of those points.

Gauff broke again for a 1-0 lead in the second set, but her serve was not as effective as Sonmez levelled at 2-2 and held three more break points for a 4-2 lead.

But a precise ace out wide and a 115mph unreturned first serve enabled Gauff to cling on in a game which you felt she would have lost a year ago.

The gutsy hold laid the platform for Gauff to immediately break for 4-3 before securing victory with another service game which displayed her belief.

Gauff hit a trio of unreturned first serves - all just under the 120mph mark, teeing up three match points as Sonmez buckled on the first after a short rally.

"Psychologically, I'm now going to go for the ace, or I know I can hit the serve and the return is probably not going to come back," said Gauff, who will play Spain's Paula Badosa or Australia's Daria Kasatkina in the second round.

"Last year I literally was like I hope I make it in. It's such a big difference knowing almost every serve I'm trying to basically hit 110, 115, 120mph if I can."
